findings.problem: The moment title - the owner's own words, the largest reading-tier object on the plan - loses 45% of its measure at one pixel of window growth and never gets it back. Measured on owner-flight and desk, paper and ink, identically: the title box is 544px (22.7em at 24px) at 900, 1000 and 1023; at 1024 it is 298px (12.4em) on owner-flight and 306px on desk; it climbs 0.92px per px of window and caps at 534px, so the 544px it had at 1023 is never regained at any width up to 1920. The cause is the two-pane composition engaging at @media (min-width:1024px): .b-plan = .b-two - 344 - 56, i.e. title = window - 726 capped at 534, so at 1024 the pane hands a 24px display-tier title 12.4em of line - narrower than the 18.8em the same title gets at 768, and half the 22.7em the same surface gives it 1px earlier. This is not cosmetic: it deletes text. Driving state=owner-editing and typing 'Champagne reception on the terrace at The Orchard, then dinner' (62 chars, an ordinary wedding line), the word-safe trimmer cuts it to 'Champagne reception on the terrace at The Orchard,' at 1024 and to '...The Orchard, then' at 1080, while the identical string sets in FULL at 768, 900, 1023, 1152, 1200, 1279 and 1440. Widening the window from 1023 to 1024 removes two words from the owner's sentence. The shipped fixture's lead moment 'Menu tasting at The Orchard' - the one object indigo marks - breaks 'Menu tasting / at The Orchard' across two lines at 1024 while setting on one at 1023 and at 1152. Identical on ink (298 vs 306px, same trim, same break), so this is not a ground-specific artifact. 1152 and 1279 are both listed frames and both still sit 22% and 2% below the 544px the same element gets at 900; 1024 - iPad landscape, the commonest tablet width an audience will open this on - is not framed at all. Not covered by any settled item: tablet-band-is-the-blown-up-phone-stack was vertical scale and its refuter conceded 'the boundary mismatch is real (geometry at 701, composition at 1024)'; keepsake-loses-the-baseline-and-the-measure-floor was print baselines; stepread-never-fits-its-measure was .b-stepRead.

biggestWin: The type system is the most disciplined thing in this artifact and it is now genuinely at the benchmark. Every size on the ramp carries its tracking on the same rule and its leading by role, and I could not find a single exception: dumping every text-bearing element across 14 states x 2 grounds x 6 widths returns exactly two families, exactly weights 400 and 600, zero italics, zero synthesised mono bold, and one letterfit and one line-height per size-and-role pair - 11px mono at 0.04em for data and 0.16em for labels, 12px at 0.20em for the ceremonial line only, 15/17/20px sans at -0.015em, 24-38px at -0.03em, and the display steps at -0.032/-0.038/-0.04/-0.05em. Two things lift it past merely consistent. First, the optical work on the count: .b-num carries a hand-set -0.05em margin to pay back Geist Mono's side bearing, and probing true ink edges with canvas metrics at 1440 puts the numeral's left ink at 186.61px against 187.00 for the 30px ceremonial date and 186.00 for the 12px label - three different families and sizes aligned to within a pixel of ink, which is the correction almost nobody makes and which is what makes the horizon read as one object rather than three stacked ones. Second, the trim is honest: it is word-safe at every width I could force it to fire, it re-runs live on every keystroke and every repaint, and across the whole matrix there is not one mid-word cut, not one widow under 30% of its line, not one element whose scrollWidth exceeds its box, and not one type metric that shifts under focus or hover. Both grounds hold the same floor - nothing sets below 0.62 on either, so the paper room is 5.31:1 and its dark twin 7.63:1 at the same ladder step, and indigo, now the primary accent, correctly never sets a word on either. That is a system, not a stylesheet, and the one defect above is the only place it does not hold.
